title: Language essentials
summary: Use values by default, optionals for absence, and descriptive generic constraints. A struct copy is independent; a class assignment shares the same instance.
note: firstMatch returns the first equal value's position. Dictionary keys and Set elements conform to Hashable; Comparable adds ordering. Use a named closure parameter when its role is not obvious.
pitfall: Never force-unwrap expected absence. inout grants temporary mutable access; increment requires an Int value below Int.max.

title: Arrays, dictionaries & sets
summary: Use defaulted dictionary subscripts for counts and reduce(into:) for a mutable accumulator. sorted returns a new array; sort mutates the existing one.
note: ArraySlice retains original indices and can retain the original allocation. Convert to Array when you need an independently owned, zero-based buffer. zip stops at the shorter input. 0..<count handles empty arrays.
pitfall: Array, Dictionary, and Set use copy-on-write: a cheap assignment can defer an O(n) copy until mutation. Hash iteration order is not a stable presentation order.
time: O(n log n) for sorting; transforms O(n) expected

title: Strings & Unicode
summary: A String is a collection of extended grapheme clusters, not an integer-indexed character array. Convert once only if the algorithm truly needs random access.
note: index(after:) advances one Character; index(_:offsetBy:) walks through characters. Array(text) gives integer indexing at the cost of a full traversal/allocation. String(substring) avoids retaining a large source buffer.
pitfall: UTF-8 offsets are bytes, not user-perceived characters. Only use byte-based alphabet tricks when ASCII is an explicit constraint. split omits empty fields by default and does not trim whitespace.
time: O(b), including conversions; b = input UTF-8 bytes

title: Math, overflow & bits
summary: Integer division truncates toward zero. Use reporting-overflow operations when limits are not guaranteed, and magnitude when Int.min is possible.
note: Euclid's algorithm works with unsigned magnitudes, including Int.min.magnitude. Rounding rules are explicit: ties-to-even differs from the default nearest-away-from-zero behavior.
pitfall: abs(Int.min) and Int.min / -1 overflow; division by zero traps. &+ wraps rather than solving overflow. A bit mask must use a shift appropriate for its integer width.
time: GCD O(log(min(a, b))) for nonzero inputs; fixed demo O(1)

title: Money: dollars & cents
summary: Store whole cents as Int, then format a Decimal amount with an explicit currency code and locale. Use an exact decimal string instead of constructing Decimal from a binary floating-point price.
note: For CAD: currencyFromCents(1999, currencyCode: "CAD", locale: Locale(identifier: "en_CA")). Locale controls separators and symbol disambiguation; the currency code identifies the unit. Display precision does not perform business-rule rounding of stored amounts.
pitfall: This cents helper assumes a currency with 100 minor units per major unit. JPY and other currencies need a different scale. Decimal also has finite precision/range; check errors for production financial arithmetic.
time: O(d) formatting work; d = output digits

title: Numbers & interpolation
summary: Use interpolation for composing strings and FormatStyle for user-facing numbers. Percent styles multiply a fractional value by 100 for display.
note: Choose a locale for deterministic examples. fractionLength(2) shows two decimal places; grouping(.never) removes separators. String(value, radix:) is useful for binary and hexadecimal representations.
pitfall: The zero-padding example is for nonnegative integers; blindly padding a negative String would place zeros before its minus sign. Avoid String(format:) when a typed FormatStyle expresses the intent.

title: Stack
summary: An Array already provides a stack: append pushes, last peeks, and popLast safely pops an optional.
note: This deliberately demonstrates LIFO storage. For reversal alone, Array(values.reversed()) avoids the extra explicit stack. popLast returns nil when empty.
pitfall: removeLast() traps on an empty array. Append is amortized O(1); a shared copy-on-write buffer can add O(n) before mutation.
time: O(n) demo; push amortized O(1), pop O(1)

title: Queue
summary: Advance a head index instead of shifting the array for every dequeue. Clear consumed references and compact only when at least half the storage is consumed.
note: The occasional O(n) compaction is charged to preceding dequeues, yielding amortized O(1) operations with uniquely owned storage. Swift Array may keep its high-water allocated capacity even after elements are released.
pitfall: A one-shot BFS can keep an ordinary array and cursor; a long-lived queue needs reference clearing/compaction. Copying this value and then mutating can trigger an O(n) copy.
time: Enqueue/dequeue amortized O(1); worst case O(n)

title: Binary heap
summary: Use a strict ordering closure: < creates a min-heap and > creates a max-heap. Heapify a batch bottom-up in linear time.
note: Only the root is guaranteed to be best; the entire backing array is not sorted. The comparator must be a consistent strict ordering. Ties have no stable insertion order.
pitfall: Do not use <= as the comparator. A value-semantic heap shares Array storage until mutation, so the usual heap operation bounds exclude a shared-buffer copy.
time: Heapify O(n); push/pop O(log n); peek O(1)
space: O(n) heap storage; O(1) sift workspace

title: Linked list & reversal
summary: Use class nodes when links represent shared identity. Reverse an acyclic singly linked list by saving the next pointer before rewiring it.
note: Reversal changes the original nodes; callers holding aliases observe rewired links. Head insertion is O(1), indexed access and lookup are O(n).
pitfall: This assumes an acyclic list. A strong next cycle can leak under ARC; adding weak indiscriminately would instead destroy normal ownership.

title: Binary tree
summary: An explicit stack visits left subtree, node, then right subtree without recursive calls. Inorder is sorted only when the tree satisfies the BST invariant.
expected: let root = TreeNode(2); root.left = TreeNode(1); inorder(root) → [1, 2]
note: A binary tree allows at most two children; a BST also orders keys. Search is O(h), which becomes O(n) for a skewed tree.
pitfall: The input must be a tree, not a cyclic graph. Stack space is O(h), not automatically O(log n). Avoid adding a strong parent pointer that forms an ownership cycle.

title: Graph representations
summary: Use vertex indices 0..<vertexCount and an array of neighbor arrays. For weighted graphs, store destination and weight together in WeightedEdge.
note: An adjacency list stores O(V + E) data; an adjacency matrix uses O(V²). Undirected edges are inserted twice. Neighbor order follows insertion order.
pitfall: The constructor requires valid vertex indices and a nonnegative vertex count. Parallel edges and self-loops are preserved, not silently deduplicated.

title: Binary search & lower bound
summary: Keep a half-open search interval [lower, upper). Lower bound returns the first index with value >= target, or count if every value is smaller.
note: The exact search checks the lower-bound candidate, so duplicate hits are deterministic. lower + (upper - lower) / 2 avoids adding the two endpoints.
pitfall: Input must be sorted ascending. Returning values.count is valid for an insertion point, but not for an Array subscript.

title: Two pointers
summary: In an ascending array, a sum below the target needs a larger left value; a sum above it needs a smaller right value.
note: The returned pair contains distinct indices, not values. Overflow direction is known when adding sorted signed integers, so the pointer moves without using the wrapped result.
pitfall: Sorting an unsorted input changes original indices and adds O(n log n). For original-index two sum on unsorted data, use a dictionary instead.

title: Sliding window
summary: Keep the last position of each Character and move the left boundary forward past a duplicate. Enumerating the String avoids materializing an indexed character array.
note: Each position enters the window once. Character equality respects Swift's Unicode semantics, so an emoji grapheme remains a single element. The result is a character count, not a UTF-8 offset.
pitfall: Do not move left backward for a duplicate already outside the window. Expected linear behavior assumes ordinary hashing; long grapheme clusters add hashing/equality work.
time: Expected O(b), b = bytes traversed/hashed; collision worst case higher
space: O(u) dictionary entries plus retained character storage

title: Prefix sums
summary: Store a leading zero, then answer sum(lower..<upper) by subtracting two prefix totals.
note: Construction allocates n + 1 totals; each query reads two array positions. The half-open convention also handles an empty range.
pitfall: Every running total AND queried subtraction must fit Int. This is a static structure: changing an input value requires rebuilding the prefixes.

title: BFS & DFS
summary: BFS marks a vertex when enqueuing it and finds shortest edge counts in an unweighted graph. DFS follows one branch before returning.
note: The BFS queue retains visited vertex indices until the function returns. DFS's visited array prevents graph cycles; its recursion depth can reach V.
pitfall: All neighbor indices and the start must be valid. An empty graph has no valid start. For adversarial deep graphs, replace recursive DFS with an explicit stack to avoid a stack overflow.
time: O(V + E) for reachable edges plus initialization
space: O(V), including BFS queue or DFS recursion

title: Dijkstra’s shortest paths
summary: For nonnegative weights, repeatedly expand the closest unsettled candidate. A better distance pushes a fresh heap entry; stale entries are skipped.
note: nil marks an unreachable vertex; Int.max remains a representable distance. Lazy duplicate heap entries make the bound O(V + E log(E + 1)), and the heap may hold O(E) candidates.
pitfall: Copy the linked heap and WeightedEdge definitions too. Negative weights/invalid vertices throw. Any explored addition overflow throws, even if a different route would fit; constrain inputs or choose a wider representation.
space: O(E + 1) heap frontier, excluding returned distances

title: Merge intervals
summary: Sort by lower bound, then merge each overlapping closed interval with the last output interval.
note: Closed intervals touching at one endpoint overlap. The resulting intervals are sorted and disjoint. Sorting's temporary storage and the copied input count toward memory use.
pitfall: 1...2 and 3...4 do not overlap here; merging adjacent integer ranges is a different policy. ClosedRange requires lowerBound <= upperBound.

title: Backtracking: subsets
summary: At each index, either skip the element or include it. Undo the inclusion before returning to the caller.
note: The output includes the empty subset. Array value semantics preserve saved results while selected mutates; copy-on-write costs are included in the output-sensitive bound.
pitfall: With duplicate input values, equal-looking subsets are produced from different positions. Exponential output cannot be made linear by memoization.

title: 1D dynamic programming
summary: best[subtotal] stores the fewest coins for that subtotal. Bottom-up evaluation makes dependencies explicit and avoids recursive stack depth.
note: Each denomination can be reused. An amount + 1 sentinel represents unreachable states. This is O(amount × coinCount), pseudo-polynomial in the numeric amount.
pitfall: Denominations must be positive and amount must be nonnegative and less than Int.max. Very large amounts can exhaust memory even when arithmetic fits. Greedy coin selection is not generally optimal.
time: O(A × C), A = amount, C = coin count

title: State & bindings
summary: The parent owns count with @State. The child receives a binding to that same value rather than making a second copy.
expected: CounterScreen() → Stepper updates the parent's solved count.
note: State storage belongs to the view's identity, not the short-lived View struct value. $count projects a Binding<Int>. Body describes UI; do not start work or mutate state while evaluating it.
pitfall: Initializing a child @State from a parent value does not establish ongoing synchronization. Changing identity resets the associated state.

title: Observation & ownership
summary: Own the observable model in @State, inject it with environment(model), and use @Bindable only where a control needs projected bindings.
expected: SessionScreen() → editing Topic and toggling Completed update the same StudySession.
note: Observation tracks properties read by a view. @Bindable supplies bindings, not ownership. @MainActor protects this UI model; @Observable by itself does not provide synchronization.
pitfall: Reading @Environment(StudySession.self) without an ancestor injection fails. A plain let reference can observe an externally owned model; not every reference needs a wrapper.

title: Identity, lists & navigation
summary: Use stable domain IDs for list rows and typed values for NavigationStack routes. An optional identifiable selection drives the sheet.
expected: TopicsScreen() → tap Heaps, then Review Heaps, then Done.
note: List(topics) uses Identifiable; ForEach(topics) uses the same stable identity contract. The typed path is the navigation state. Dismiss comes from the sheet's own environment.
pitfall: Do not generate a fresh UUID every time an id is read. An array offset is not a stable ID for movable content. Mutable route payloads can become stale snapshots.

title: Layout & accessible controls
summary: Compose semantic Text, Label, and Button views, using relative text styles and layouts that can grow vertically.
expected: ReviewSummary(completed: 3, review: {}) → labeled full-width review button.
note: Parents propose a size; children choose a size; parents place them. Modifier order matters: padding before frame differs from padding after frame. A button label already gives an accessible action name.
pitfall: Avoid fixed text heights and tiny icon-only tap targets. accessibilityLabel replaces the spoken label; use it when the visible content is insufficient, not redundantly on every Text.

title: Tasks & cancellation
summary: Attach work to the view with .task(id:). SwiftUI cancels it when the ID changes or the view disappears; the work must cooperate with cancellation.
expected: TopicSearchScreen() → entering "he" displays Heap after a short debounce.
note: Task.sleep suspends without blocking. A cancellation check prevents an obsolete result from updating state. The tiny in-memory list is intentional demo data, not an external service stub.
pitfall: async does not mean background execution. This filter runs on the main actor and is suitable only for small data. Move heavy work to an explicitly concurrent boundary rather than blocking the UI.

title: Existing-code ownership
summary: For an ObservableObject model, @StateObject owns a persistent instance and @ObservedObject observes a borrowed one. Modern examples prefer Observation.
expected: LegacyOwner() → the child button increments the shared LegacyCounter.
note: These APIs remain useful when reading older code; they are not all deprecated. With @Observable, the rough ownership counterparts are @State and a plain reference, with @Bindable when bindings are required.
pitfall: Constructing an owned model inline in an @ObservedObject declaration can recreate it when its parent rebuilds the view value.

title: UIKit inside SwiftUI
summary: Create UIKit objects once in makeUIView/makeUIViewController; synchronize mutable inputs in update methods.
note: ShareSheet treats text as immutable for one presentation, so its update method is intentionally empty. For delegate-to-binding communication, retain a Coordinator via makeCoordinator and refresh its input references in update.
pitfall: Do not create a new UIKit view during every update or mutate SwiftUI state synchronously from updateUIView. If the share payload changes, present a new sheet identity.

title: View & controller lifecycle
summary: Use viewDidLoad for one-time view setup, appearance callbacks for visibility-dependent work, and layout callbacks for bounds-dependent geometry.
expected: LifecycleController().loadViewIfNeeded() → one status label; repeated layout adds no subviews.
note: UIView.layoutSubviews concerns that view's geometry; UIViewController.viewDidLayoutSubviews runs after its root view lays out. viewDidAppear is appropriate when a completed presentation matters.
pitfall: Layout can run many times. Do not rebuild constraints, fetch data, or append child views on every pass. Always call the superclass lifecycle implementation.

title: Auto Layout & priorities
summary: Constrain against the safe area and disable autoresizing-mask translation on manually constrained views. Use priorities to express which view should stretch or shrink.
expected: ProfileController() → a Name label and an expanding text field.
note: Higher hugging resists growing beyond intrinsic size; higher compression resistance resists shrinking below it. UIStackView manages its arranged-subview constraints. Dynamic Type fonts can resize.
pitfall: Too many required constraints can conflict. Horizontal rows are compact examples, not a promise of ideal layout at every accessibility text size; use vertical arrangements when content no longer fits.

title: Diffable lists & stable IDs
summary: Register reusable cells once, outside the provider closure. A diffable snapshot contains stable item identifiers; fetch mutable display data by identifier.
expected: TopicsController().renameTopic(id: 2, title: "Priority queues") → the same item updates.
note: Keep the data source strongly owned. reconfigureItems updates content without changing identity. IndexPath is a current position and can change after snapshot edits.
pitfall: Recreating CellRegistration inside the provider undermines reuse. Duplicate identifiers violate the snapshot contract. Avoid capturing a controller strongly in a closure it owns.

title: Reusable cells & async work
summary: Cancel the previous load on every configuration, reset visible content, and validate both item identity and request generation before applying a result.
expected: ThumbnailCell.configure(id: 1, loadImage: { UIImage() }) → replaces the placeholder for that request only.
note: The injected loader makes the example testable. A request token also protects same-item reconfiguration. Call cancelLoad from the table delegate's didEndDisplaying callback when work should stop offscreen.
pitfall: Cancellation alone does not force arbitrary loaders to stop. Do not use IndexPath as request identity. Keep heavy image decoding off the main actor even though UI updates happen there.

title: Delegation & ARC
summary: A coordinator owns its picker; the picker holds only a weak reference back to its class-bound delegate.
note: Weak references are optional and become nil when the object deallocates. The protocol is @MainActor because callbacks mutate UI-owned state. The owner must retain the coordinator for as long as it is needed.
pitfall: weak is an ownership decision, not a default on every reference. unowned crashes if its lifetime assumption is wrong. A strong closure stored by its own captured object can create another cycle.

title: Push, present & dismiss
summary: Push onto a navigation stack for hierarchical detail. Present a separate controller for a modal task, and dismiss it when the task completes.
expected: Embed NavigationExampleController in UINavigationController; call pushDetail() or presentReview().
note: The optional navigationController is nil unless the controller is embedded. A sheet wraps its own navigation controller to display the Done button.
pitfall: A presented controller's action can form a cycle if it strongly captures that controller. The weak capture here breaks that ownership loop. UIKit UI work stays on the main actor.

title: SwiftUI inside UIKit
summary: Wrap a SwiftUI view in UIHostingController and follow the complete child-controller containment sequence.
expected: HostingExampleController() → SwiftUI Text fills its safe-area container.
note: addChild establishes controller ownership, adding the view establishes view hierarchy, constraints establish geometry, and didMove completes containment.
pitfall: To remove a child, call willMove(toParent: nil), remove its view, then removeFromParent(). Adding only the hosted view skips lifecycle propagation.
